venues.d: The grande dame of them all — a courtyard garden hidden behind the city's most powerful street.
The Four Seasons standard our members already trust, wrapped in legendary flowers.
Starck's hand over an 18th-century bones, looking straight onto the gardens.
The couture address — Dior at the door and the red awnings on the avenue.

venues.a: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
venues.d: LVMH's newest icon — river light, a Dior spa, and a pool most hotels can only envy.

venues.n: Hôtel de Crillon, A Rosewood Hotel
venues.d: An 18th-century palace on the grandest square, restored without losing its nerve.

venues.a: 8th arr. / near the Arc de Triomphe
venues.d: The artist's palace — Starck design, its own gallery and cinema, a long quiet pool.

venues.a: 8th arr. / Avenue Gabriel, by the Élysée
venues.d: A forty-key mansion that feels less like a hotel and more like a private house.
A Bonaparte prince's palace, with the Eiffel Tower filling many of the windows.

venues.a: 16th arr. / near the Arc de Triomphe
venues.d: Peninsula precision and a rooftop that trades on the finest view in Paris.
Italian glamour dropped onto the smartest corner, with one of the city's largest hotel spas.
The only Palace on the Left Bank — literary Saint-Germain in an Art Deco landmark.
Family-owned Barrière glamour above the most famous brasserie on the avenue.
The most famous hotel name in the world, still keeping the promise on Place Vendôme.
A discreet townhouse near the Élysée for members who prefer to be unseen.

venues.a: 16th arr. / near the Bois de Boulogne
venues.d: The only château-hotel in Paris, set behind its own gardens.
A garden courtyard hidden off the smartest shopping street, run to the group's quiet precision.
Refined and understated, a calm base a step from the jewellers of Vendôme.
Italian-run, jewel-box luxury on the Left Bank — warm where the palaces can be grand.
A chic forty-five-key house between the Louvre and the Palais Royal.
Starck-designed and buzzing, with a rooftop garden and a fashionable crowd.
Elegant, intimate and perfectly placed for a day among the maisons.
Refined and central, with a spa and a Michelin-recognised kitchen of its own.
A fashion-crowd design hotel that hides its glamour behind a plain door.
Belle Époque opulence and a La Mer spa, tucked into the Marais.
Joyful maximalism and one of the liveliest hotel restaurants in town.
A garden-inspired newcomer with a rooftop and a light-hearted spirit.
Sleek and discreet, arranged around a quiet courtyard.
Hidden behind the loveliest square in Paris — romantic and quiet.
A warm, well-placed boutique with more soul than its size suggests.

venues.a: 1st arr. / by the Palais Royal gardens
venues.d: Elegant and superbly placed, a step from the arcades of the Palais Royal.
A hushed Left Bank townhouse built around its own courtyard.
A Japanese hand on French cooking, exact to the millimetre — one of the city's nine three-stars.

venues.a: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
venues.d: Sauces treated as the whole point, in a room that looks out over the river.
The garden on the plate — Passard's near-vegan turn is the finest veg-friendly table at this height.
Classical French haute in a palace dining room — the grand occasion, done properly.
French haute cuisine facing Le Bristol's garden — serene, precise, timeless.

venues.a: 8th arr. / Rue Balzac, near the Champs-Élysées
venues.d: The avant-garde of modern French cooking, three stars held since 1996.
Intimate three-star cooking inside one of the city's most private houses.
A pavilion in the Champs-Élysées gardens, and Alléno's modern French at full stretch.
A belle-époque pavilion set deep in the park — one of the loveliest tables in Paris.

venues.n: Restaurant Guy Savoy – Monnaie de Paris
venues.a: 6th arr. / on the Seine, the former Mint
venues.d: The most-decorated name in the city by La Liste, in a riverside palace.
The international ticket of the moment — produce-led cooking from the counter.
Old-guard grandeur on the most beautiful square in Paris.
A private mansion, a Bordeaux cellar to match, and cooking of real depth.
Stéphanie Le Quellec's precise modern French — one of the city's top kitchens.
Vegetable-forward modern French, curious and quietly brilliant.
A grande-maison institution, classical to its bones.
A jewel-box room and Piège's exacting modern French.
The George V's lighter, luminous second table — no less serious for it.
A sushi counter of rare finesse, within Alléno's pavilion.
French cooking on the rooftop, with the Eiffel Tower for company.
Dinner inside the Eiffel Tower itself — the view every first visit wants.
Old-school luxury and classical French in Art Nouveau rooms.

venues.a: 5th arr. / Left Bank, near the Seine
venues.d: Restrained, precise modern French with none of the theatre.
An omakase counter working with fish of exceptional quality.
The most coveted mid-price reservation in Paris — seasonal, confident, warm.
Greg Marchand's intimate, buzzing bistronomy — small room, big following.
The only Michelin-starred bistro in Paris — Belle Époque, and run by Ducasse.
Escargots, sole meunière and a 1900s room — the Paris bistro, preserved.
The one genuinely Michelin-listed Indian in Paris — refined, and never a cliché.

venues.a: 6th arr. / Rue Dauphine, near Pont Neuf
venues.d: A glamorous Indian bistro on the Left Bank with real vegetarian breadth.
The cult bistronomy address — a small counter that shaped a whole movement.
A lively Basque institution — generous cooking and a legendary riz au lait.
The birthplace of bistronomy, still personal, still priced with restraint.
Produce and wine of unusual seriousness, in a warm neighbourhood room.
Surprise tasting menus at an open kitchen — French technique, Korean soul.
The bistro of the imagination — steak-frites, soufflé, a wall of wine.
Septime's seafood sibling — small plates, natural wine, no reservations.
The Levha sisters' playful pan-Asian — bright, fun, generous.
Warm bistronomy and a blackboard menu, at a price that flatters the cooking.
Creative small plates and natural wine in an easy, buzzy room.
Simple French cooking done exactly right — the food a French grandmother would make.
A 1940s bistro mood and a short, seasonal menu that rarely misses.
Seasonal bistro cooking and a terrace that looks straight at the tower.
French comfort cooking with real value — a neighbourhood room worth the trip.
A Franco-Japanese couple's regional French, touched lightly by Japan.
A flavour tour of Laos and Thailand, credentialed and unpretentious.
A 1939 institution of Breton-leaning bistronomy, in a Japanese chef's careful hands.
Cantonese cooking done cleanly and well, in the heart of Paris's Chinatown.
A tiny counter given over to Korean dumplings, made with real care.
The city's iron heart; go to the summit at dusk and catch the on-the-hour sparkle, or dine at the Jules Verne on the second floor for a table above Paris.
Climb the 284 steps to a rooftop where twelve avenues fan out like a star, with the Champs-Élysées running straight to the Louvre.
Reopened December 2024 after the 2019 fire, the restored nave gleams brighter than in living memory; entry is free, and the bell towers reopened in September 2025 for the climb to the gargoyles.
A jewel-box royal chapel where fifteen soaring windows of 13th-century stained glass wrap you in coloured light — go on a bright morning for the full effect.
The white domed basilica crowns the highest point in Paris; the steps below give one of the great free panoramas, and the dome climb rewards with a 360° sweep.
A neoclassical temple where France buries its greats — Voltaire, Curie, Hugo — with Foucault's pendulum swinging under the dome and a colonnade viewpoint above.
Under the gilded dome lies Napoleon in six nested coffins; the complex also holds the Army Museum, strong on the family history-of-France angle.
The most opulent theatre in Europe — grand staircase, gilded foyer, and a Chagall-painted ceiling; tour it by day or take an advisor-booked box for a ballet.
The world's largest art museum; ask us to arrange an early-access or after-hours private hour so you meet the Mona Lisa and Venus de Milo without the crush.
A grand Beaux-Arts railway station turned temple of Impressionism — Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh, Degas — best from the giant golden clock window on the top floor.
Two oval rooms hold Monet's monumental Water Lilies, wrapping you in eight curved panels designed by the painter himself — a meditative, unhurried half-hour.
The sculptor's mansion and rose garden, where The Thinker and The Kiss sit among clipped hedges — one of the loveliest, calmest museums in the city, ideal with children.
A restored 17th-century mansion in the Marais holding the world's greatest Picasso collection, drawn from the artist's own estate.
The inside-out building of coloured pipes houses Europe's biggest modern-art museum; note it is closing for a multi-year renovation, so confirm access with us before you plan.
François Pinault's contemporary art inside a domed former grain exchange reimagined by Tadao Ando — a concrete cylinder within a historic rotunda; the 2026 show 'Clair-obscur' runs into late August.
The world's largest Monet holding, including 'Impression, Sunrise' — the painting that named the movement — in an intimate townhouse well off the tourist track.

venues.n: Musée du Quai Branly — Jacques Chirac
venues.d: Jean Nouvel's museum of the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, wrapped in a living green wall — a thoughtful, less-obvious stop near the Eiffel Tower.
The city's fine-arts museum in a jewel of a 1900 building — free entry, a gilded interior, and a serene garden café most visitors walk right past.
Reopened in 2024 after a sweeping restoration, its vast glass-and-iron nave is Paris's grandest exhibition hall — check what blockbuster show is on.
A perfectly preserved aristocratic mansion of 18th-century French decorative arts, with a moving family history — a quiet gem beside Parc Monceau.
A collector couple's opulent townhouse hung with Italian and French masters; take tea in the frescoed dining room under a Tiepolo ceiling.
The best-preserved old quarter — Renaissance mansions, the arcaded Place des Vosges, designer boutiques and falafel lanes; wander with no plan, it rewards it.
Literary Left Bank of Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots, antique galleries and the city's oldest church — the neighbourhood for a slow morning and good browsing.
The village on the hill — cobbled lanes, the last working vineyard in Paris, artists in Place du Tertre, and hidden squares away from the crowds if you climb early.
A serene 17th-century island in the Seine, one main street of mansions and small shops — stroll the quays with a Berthillon ice cream, a Paris rite.
Iron footbridges, plane trees and locks lined with young Paris; walk the canal to Bassin de la Villette, or take a slow boat cruise through the underground vaults.
Student Paris around the Sorbonne, plus the sloping market street of Rue Mouffetard — one of the oldest in the city, lined with cheese, wine and produce stalls.
The most beloved park in Paris — sail a toy boat on the fountain, watch a puppet show, and sit in the green chairs among statues and orchards; children adore it.
The grand formal garden linking the Louvre to Place de la Concorde; ponds, statues and, in summer, a fairground with a big wheel over the treetops.
A hidden arcaded courtyard behind the Louvre — Buren's striped columns, lime-tree walks and old-world boutiques; one of the quietest lovely corners in the centre.
The most dramatic park in Paris — cliffs, a lake, a temple on a crag and a suspension bridge; a local, family-filled escape far from the tourist centre.

venues.n: Bois de Boulogne & Fondation Louis Vuitton
venues.d: Paris's great western woodland for boating and gardens, now anchored by Frank Gehry's glass-sail Fondation Louis Vuitton — a landmark of art and architecture in itself.
A hilly garden-necropolis of cobbled avenues and grand tombs — Chopin, Wilde, Piaf, Jim Morrison; strangely peaceful and beautiful, especially in autumn.
Under the great stained-glass dome of the flagship store, then up to the free rooftop terrace for one of the best open-air views of the Opéra and Eiffel Tower.
The one skyline view that includes the Eiffel Tower — the 56th-floor deck and open rooftop give the finest sunset panorama in the city, minus the queues of the tower itself.
Glass-roofed 19th-century arcades — Galerie Vivienne, Passage des Panoramas, Passage Jouffroy — full of mosaic floors, old bookshops and tearooms; a rainy-day treasure hunt.
One of the liveliest, most authentic markets — a covered hall of fine cheese and produce plus an open-air flea market; go with us for a chef-led tasting stroll.
A pretty pedestrian market street of cheesemongers, bakeries and florists near the Eiffel Tower — the classic spot to assemble a picnic for the Champ de Mars.
The world's largest antiques market — a sprawling maze of dealer stands in vintage furniture, art and curiosities; an advisor guide makes the labyrinth worthwhile.
The green riverside book boxes are a UNESCO-listed Paris institution — browse antique prints, posters and old books along the quays between the bridges.
Glide past the floodlit monuments over a fine dinner; we book the private or premium boats — and can arrange a fully vegetarian or Jain-aware menu on board.
The couture spine of Paris — Dior, Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Valentino — flagship after flagship; we can arrange private in-store appointments and after-hours access.
From Colette concept-store cool to the high-jewellery houses of Place Vendôme — Cartier, Van Cleef, Boucheron — set around the Ritz; the address for jewels and watches.
The world's first department store and still the most refined — with La Grande Épicerie next door for one of the great food halls in Paris.
A former foundry turned immersive digital art hall where masterpieces sweep across the walls and floor to music — a hit with children and the whole family.
The elevated garden walkway on a disused railway viaduct — the inspiration for New York's High Line — running above the arch-shops of the Viaduc des Arts.
Jean Nouvel's silver concert hall with world-class acoustics; we secure seats for an evening of the Orchestre de Paris or a visiting name.
Descend into a vaulted stone cellar like Caveau de la Huchette or Le Duc des Lombards for late live jazz — an intimate, only-in-Paris night out.
The supreme royal palace — Hall of Mirrors, the State Apartments, and vast formal gardens with the musical fountain shows; ask us for a private guide and skip-the-line timing.
A fairytale château in a moat, holding the finest old-master collection outside the Louvre, plus the Great Stables and a Le Nôtre park — quieter than Versailles.
A royal residence for eight centuries, from Francis I to Napoleon — sumptuous, uncrowded, and set in a vast forest ideal for a family walk or ride.
Twenty-five seats, a legend at the shaker, and the most storied cocktail room in Paris.
The highest-ranked bar in Paris right now — Art Nouveau brought to life, drink by drink.
A British pub reimagined by serious bartenders — warm, unpretentious, world-class.
Velvet and gold in a covered arcade — precise cocktails behind Daniele Dalla Pola's counter.
For a decade one of the world's most decorated bars — conceptual menus, faultless execution.
The bar that began the Paris speakeasy era — a taqueria out front, a hidden room behind.
French spirits only — Cognac, Calvados, Armagnac — behind a deliberately shabby door.
Franck Audoux's study of pre-1930s French cocktails, in a listed Art Nouveau corner house.
A female-led room, light and green, from alumni of the Experimental Cocktail Club.

venues.a: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
venues.d: The seventh-floor terrace of an LVMH palace, from Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower.
A glass rooftop under Jean Nouvel's roof, with the Eiffel Tower almost close enough to touch.
